add.text:
Read this numbered, cleaned transcript of the owner talking. Turn it into an outline a reader
takes in at a glance: "tangible, familiar, easy to digest". The owner's words for it: "putting
familiar names, like the headings" on the thing being discussed and on each of its parts.

Output Markdown in EXACTLY this shape:

# <the concrete thing being discussed>
## <a familiar name for one part of it>
- <one point, in the owner's own words> [S#, S#]
  - <a detail or example of that point, only if it needs its own line> [S#]
## <the next part>
- <...> [S#]

Rules:
- The H1 is CONCRETE: a thing a reader could point at — a class, a page, a tab, a tool, a feature
  (the owner's example: "Page class"). Never an abstract category like "AI processes", "Thoughts"
  or "Feedback". If the transcript covers several separate things, name them plainly in the one
  H1 ("Page class and Sidebar") and give each its own H2 or H2s.
- Exactly ONE "#" H1. One "##" H2 per distinct part — never invent one just to have more.
- Each H2 is a FAMILIAR name a reader already knows. If a name already exists for that part (the
  owner's example: "Layout"), use that exact name; otherwise use the owner's own word for it.
- ONE BULLET PER POINT, NOT PER SENTENCE. When several sentences make one point (a claim, its
  reason, "so I like that"), merge them into one bullet, a short line in the owner's own words,
  citing every one of those sentences. Filler that makes no point of its own ("Couple of things.")
  gets no bullet: add its number to the nearest bullet's citation instead.
- AT MOST TWO LEVELS: a bullet, and sub-bullets under it. Never a third level.
- KEEP EVERY POINT. Merging sentences that make the same point is required; dropping a point is
  not allowed. Never turn a hedge ("maybe", "I think", "I guess") into a flat claim.
- Cite EVERY sentence number EXACTLY ONCE, in the one bullet where its main point went — never
  under two headings. Form: [S3, S7], each number individually, never a range like [S6-S9]. Use
  only numbers that appear below.

STYLE of anything the owner will read (the owner's rules):
- It is an OVERVIEW of what was said, in the owner's own key words. Never the whole rant, never a retelling.
- Each point has its answer or action baked in: say what is done, what to do, or what is still open. Do not invent an answer the transcript or the facts do not give; mark such a point open instead.
- Order by dependency and ease: clarifications and quick items first, then what depends on them. If neither applies, keep the owner's order.
- Reuse the same names for the same things every time, so they become familiar, and always name the context (the page, class, module or session) a point belongs to.
- Headings are big: "#" for the one subject, "##" for each part, "###" only when a part truly needs a split. Never "####" or smaller. Every heading starts with one fitting emoji icon.
- Under a heading: short titled lists. A status bullet starts with ✅ (done) or ⬜ (not done) when the status is known; otherwise a plain "-" bullet. Few emoji, never decoration.
- Every card cites the clean-sentence numbers it came from, like [S3, S7], each number individually.
Apply this to the headings and bullets of the outline.

Cleaned transcript:
"""

S3. So, I mean, the way that the chat bubbles are then sent to the smart assistant, I'd like to be able to see a little bit better when they get sent.
S4. So maybe the green check mark.
S5. I don't know what the green check mark right now is supposed to be.
S6. I think there was some sort of clarity situation or feature or whatever, where if the sentence made sense, it would get a green check mark.
S7. Make sense it would get a yellow question mark
S8. I still think something like that could be useful, however.
S9. Well, we just need a cent UI
S10. And a green check mark seems to be maybe the way to do it.
S11. Although another way to do that is to chunk chat bubbles into different chat bubbles.
S12. So when the UI decides via pause or via a sentence chunk to send off to the smart assistant...
S13. Well, okay.
S14. I mean, there's two layers.
S15. There's the fast assistant should get every sentence.
S16. And then the smart assistant should get...
S17. Well, my thinking last night was that the fast assistant would have to, well, maybe it's on a new paragraph kind of instruction.
S18. It automatically happens.
S19. So, I mean, that actually makes sense.
S20. In the... I don't know if we have the session instantiated server side, but I think we could and should.
S21. If we don't already.
S22. Check into that.
S23. And then if it is instantiated server side, we could have some code so that when a new paragraph essentially is created via the fast assistant.
S24. So the fast assistant gets each sentence.
S25. It either it places it with the last paragraph or a new paragraph
S26. And frankly, every time you send an interjection, while I'm talking or if you send an update.
S27. Then that should probably, I don't know if I should split my paragraph or if my... okay, I think if I'm still transcribing to the last paragraph, my paragraph should move below.
S28. So that, well, as I'm dictating in real time, it's updating and so it should kind of move to the bottom of the list.
S29. That effect of bringing, resurfacing things and removing them
S30. I think if it's within the last few seconds, changing the order isn't necessarily a problem because it's sort of just more... Well, it's more of a user interface tweak than a... we don't want to necessarily restructure the logs by pulling things out of place every time.
S31. So I... and I don't know if this made it into the system.
S32. We don't necessarily have to design this first.
S33. What we're working on
S34. The shape of how to reference something from the past is that you could...
S35. Well, for one, you could move it in a way that's, if you wanted to move a past chat card or task or whatever back to the bottom of the list for reference or whatever, you could move it essentially where you... move it with a little arrow that, well, it could dim itself in its original place, so it, the presence of it in its original home, we don't necessarily want to remove things from their context, it's like it was created here, and this, if you scroll up you can see the chat that produced it essentially or whatever
S36. And then when you click on it, well, so if it was moved, it could have a little arrow overlay that, and it could be dimmed out, meaning, hey, this thing's not here.
S37. It's been moved.
S38. You click on the thing or the arrow and it jumps, scrolls to the new location in the chat.
S39. So that'd be one way to kind of reorder things for, resurfacing it for my attention, or, well, if it's completed, for example, maybe that's how we, when we complete tasks, like, you of making it seem like a duplicate, it gets moved from its original home
S40. And then also in the new home, whenever it's referenced, the same kind of arrow overlay could kind of be in reverse, like a back arrow, showing, hey, this was moved from another location.
S41. That seems like a pretty complex outcome.
S42. I'm not sure if that's the way to do it.
S43. Let me slow down here and try and catch up on these responses.
S44. So you need to write down, we need to, number one, the smart assistant here, you are a mastermind.
S45. You need to be getting as much done that I'm saying and try to move things forward when I'm doing my best to try and articulate what needs to happen here because we've got a lot of work to do, but I don't read all of your responses.
S46. So, yeah, this proposal here, it's, I don't know if...
"""

Output ONLY the Markdown described above (the H1, its H2s, and their bullets), nothing else.
